extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in computational linguistics / natural language processing interested in computational humour and incongruity detection
extracted.subtask_description: Automatic identification of the humorous punch line among plausible continuations of a joke set-up, using measures of semantic relatedness and joke-specific features. Evaluation is based on selecting the single comic continuation from multiple coherent endings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity-resolution theory (humour basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Incongruity resolution is one of the most widely accepted theories of humour, suggesting that humour is due to the mixing of two disparate interpretation frames in one statement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models for humour detection should operationalize the notion of mixing or clash between interpretation frames — i.e., detect when two disparate semantic/interpretive frames are combined in a single utterance in a way that produces a comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task definition: punch-line identification among plausible endings
rubrics_metrics.description: The task is redefined as the automatic identification of the humorous punch line among all the plausible endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should measure a model's ability to pick the single comic continuation from a set of plausible continuations for a given set-up (e.g., accuracy in selecting the humorous ending). Dataset examples should present a set-up followed by multiple coherent continuations with only one comic option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset design: set-ups with four continuations (one comic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new data set consisting of a series of 'set-ups' (preparations for a punch line), each of them followed by four possible coherent continuations out of which only one has a comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building or using evaluation data, ensure continuations are all plausible/coherent (to make the task non-trivial) and that only one continuation produces the comic effect. This supports clear supervised evaluation (multi-choice selection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of measures of semantic relatedness as model components
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper explores several measures of semantic relatedness ... and tries to understand their appropriateness as computational models for incongruity detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multiple semantic relatedness/similarity methods (e.g., latent semantic analysis, WordNet-based measures, information-content measures, PMI-IR/SVD-based approaches) and evaluate how well each captures the semantic distance or clash indicative of incongruity. Compare and analyze which measures correspond to comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of joke-specific features
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of joke-specific features are explored alongside semantic relatedness measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and include features tailored to joke structure or pragmatic markers of humour (unspecified on the page but implied). Evaluate whether these specialized features improve identification of the punch line relative to general semantic relatedness measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model appropriateness for incongruity detection (evaluation principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The work aims to 'try to understand [the measures'] appropriateness as computational models for incongruity detection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge models not only by raw selection accuracy but by how well their signals map to the theoretical notion of incongruity (e.g., whether high semantic distance between set-up and punchline, or a particular pattern of feature activations, corresponds to human judgments of incongruity). Use qualitative analysis and error analysis to assess theoretical fit.
